place: Rubaya (Masisi, North Kivu) and Lomera (Kabare, South Kivu)
unit: artisanal miners killed
summary: Amnesty documented the summary killing of 18 artisanal miners by M23 fighters or mine security guards working with M23: 10 beaten to death, 2 shot at point-blank range, 6 abducted and later found dead.

unit: miners died of beating injuries
summary: A health worker and a rights defender in Masisi told Amnesty that seven miners died at a health centre after being beaten by M23 fighters or their collaborators.

unit: miner killed
summary: M23 killed a miner from Walungu at Lomera, which set off a miners' uprising in which M23 offices were destroyed; M23 suspended mining there on 30 Aug 2025.

unit: % of summary executions recorded nationwide attributed to AFC/M23
summary: UN human-rights statistics given to the Group of Experts showed summary executions were the most frequently documented violation; AFC/M23 was the main perpetrator, with about 45% of them, and over 30% of all documented violations.

unit: civilians killed (over)
summary: During joint RDF and AFC/M23 operations against FDLR-linked areas, UN and humanitarian sources reported over 300 civilians killed in Bwito alone, including through targeted executions. Context only: farming areas, not mines.
Former recruits told the Group of Experts of systematic torture and executions in AFC/M23 training camps, notably Rumangabo, including of conscripts who tried to desert.

The Group of Experts found VDP/Wazalendo groups carried out summary executions and targeted killings of people accused of colluding with AFC/M23, on a much smaller scale than AFC/M23 and RDF; ANCDH fighters were most often implicated in abuses.

unit: children killed (519) or maimed (399)
summary: The UN verified the killing or maiming of 918 children; M23 was attributed 404, CODECO 109, FARDC 100, Nyatura 66, FDLR-FOCA 15, Wazalendo 13.

perpetrator: M23 and collaborating mine security guards
unit: diggers in one tunnel (miner's estimate)
summary: A Rubaya digger told Amnesty he worked a week underground with more than 150 others, sleeping about two hours a night on minimal food; when he asked to leave he was beaten by guards working with M23 and paid a fraction of the agreed wage.

Amnesty found forced labour common at M23-controlled mines: detained miners who could not pay ransoms were made to dig for M23, and others were kept for days or weeks underground for little or no pay. One man who reported his brother's killing was made to dig for M23 for over two weeks.

unit: miners held in a pit (more than)
summary: Amnesty documented underground detention pits (ndake, about 1.5-2 m deep and covered); more than 20 Rubaya miners were held in one and beaten three times a day.

perpetrator: M23 and collaborating mine security guards
unit: of 26 interviewees reported torture or ill-treatment
summary: Sixteen of the 26 people Amnesty interviewed said M23 or its mine guards had tortured or ill-treated them, including beatings for asking for breaks or refusing to hand over ore.
The Group of Experts found Zaïre commander Baraka Maki Amos imposed 'salongo' forced labour and illegal taxes in the Mabanga gold area, punishing non-compliance.

The US Labor Department's TVPRA list names DRC cobalt, copper, diamonds, gold, coltan, cassiterite and wolframite as produced with child labour; gold, coltan, cassiterite and wolframite also with forced child labour and forced labour; cobalt also with forced labour.

DoL says children aged 5-17 are reported forced to work in coltan, cassiterite and wolframite mines in the Kivus, some in debt bondage with families, and that mines controlled by armed groups or military officers round up villagers to work. It gives 'thousands' for gold and 'hundreds' for wolframite, not counts.
paragraph_or_page: DRC coltan, tin, tungsten, gold rows

unit: % of children aged 5-14 working (all sectors)
summary: DoL's 2024 Findings list forced mining of gold, coltan, cassiterite and wolframite and use of children in mineral smuggling among the worst forms of child labour in the DRC; 17.4% of children aged 5-14 work (all sectors, not mining only).

unit: % of working children aged 5-14 in industry (incl. mining)
summary: DoL's Rwanda Findings say children do dangerous tasks in informal mining, including carrying heavy loads, and list forced labour in mining among categorical worst forms; industry, which includes mining and construction, accounts for 3.2% of working children aged 5-14.

unit: children among the dead (about)
summary: The DRC Ministry of Mines said about 70 minors were among more than 200 dead in the 3 Mar 2026 Rubaya collapse, which shows children were working at the site. Already in seed (TV5MONDE/Mongabay).

place: Eastern DRC (North Kivu 676, South Kivu 537, Ituri 300 victims)
unit: CRSV victims verified by the UN
summary: The UN verified 887 CRSV cases affecting 1,534 victims in eastern DRC in 2025 (854 women, 672 girls, 4 men, 4 boys), up 59% on cases from 2024. Armed groups were responsible for 75% of victims (M23 first, then CODECO, Wazalendo, Mai-Mai) and state agents for 19% (FARDC first).

unit: documented cases implicating M23 in 2025 (152 in 2024)
summary: The Secretary-General reports that cases implicating M23, including rape, gang rape and sexual slavery, rose from 152 in 2024 to 439 in 2025, often against people seen as linked to FARDC or Wazalendo.

unit: cases implicating FARDC
summary: Of 305 cases attributed to state actors in 2025, 285 implicated the FARDC, 60% more than in 2024, including rape during looting as troops withdrew in South Kivu.

unit: victims (60 women, 17 girls)
summary: Sexual violence against 60 women and 17 girls in the Kivus was attributed to groups operating under the Wazalendo label; the Group of Experts also verified a sharp rise in CRSV in government- and Wazalendo-held South Kivu.

place: North Kivu, South Kivu, Ituri, Maniema, Tanganyika
unit: sexual-violence cases registered by service providers
summary: Service providers registered 90,199 sexual-violence cases in five eastern provinces in Jan-Sep 2025, mainly by armed actors. These are care records, not UN-verified cases.

unit: children (589 girls, 3 boys)
summary: The UN verified sexual violence against 592 children; FARDC was attributed 147, M23 124, CODECO 69, Nyatura 38, Mai-Mai Yakotumba 23.

The Group of Experts found AFC/M23 inspectors sought aggregate and patient-level sexual-violence data from health facilities and called published figures invented, which may deter survivors and cut recorded cases in 2026.

unit: young men incl. minors taken (more than)
summary: The DRC human rights minister said more than 300 young men, including minors, were seized in Rubaya and taken to an unknown destination; the Group of Experts says local sources, civil society and eyewitnesses confirmed the incident.

unit: miners interviewed who described recruitment threats
summary: Seven miners told Amnesty that M23 detained miners and threatened to send them to the Rumangabo or Tchanzou training camps unless ransoms were paid; one saw M23 trucks leave Lomera full of miners heading to camps.

unit: young men rounded up (about)
summary: During a cordon-and-search, AFC/M23 seized about 80 young men suspected of Wazalendo links, put them in AFC/M23 uniforms and sent them to the front as human shields, per the Group of Experts.

unit: children recruited and used
summary: The UN verified 1,397 children recruited and used; M23 142, Wazalendo 34, Nyatura 84, Raia Mutomboki 79, NDC-R 9, APCLS 7, FARDC 1, plus many Mai-Mai groups; 1,067 children were abducted, 570 by M23.

unit: children recruited and used (UN-verified, per DoL)
summary: DoL reports M23 recruited children with false job offers, trained them in Rwanda and Uganda and sent them into combat; it also says FARDC supported FDLR, APCLS, NDC-R and other Wazalendo groups that recruited children.

unit: internally displaced persons
summary: The Group of Experts, citing OCHA key figures for 31 Mar 2026, reports 3.4 million IDPs across Ituri and North and South Kivu.

unit: newly displaced (more than)
summary: More than 100,000 people were newly displaced within Masisi in early 2025 by fighting between FARDC and allies and AFC/M23 and RDF.
M23 told residents not originally from the area to leave the Lomera site in March 2026 and then demolished their structures; satellite imagery from June 2026 shows many structures gone.
Alphamin's Bisie tin mine suspended operations from 13 March to mid-April 2025 as AFC/M23 advanced on Walikale; resumption coincided with the withdrawal.

unit: USD per kg coltan (USD 2 per kg cassiterite)
summary: AFC/M23 levies a per-kilogram tax at sale, about $4/kg for coltan and $2/kg for cassiterite, and invoices it in Rubaya and Mubambiro; transporters pay after delivery into an Equity Bank account of its provincial finance coordinator.

unit: USD per year artisanal miner licence (traders USD 250)
summary: AFC/M23 charges artisanal miners $25 a year and local traders $250, plus FC 500 a day for day labourers, transporters and petty traders to enter the site.

unit: USD per kg coltan said to go to the Rwandan government (plus USD 4 to M23)
summary: Amnesty reports that traders pay $4/kg to M23 and $3/kg to the Rwandan government on coltan, citing UN and Global Witness work.

unit: % production tax on ore sale price at pit
summary: After taking Lomera in mid-February 2025, AFC/M23 set up its own 'mining office' and imposed a 30% production tax on the pit-level sale price, plus fees on crushers and other actors. Over 5,000 artisanal miners worked there in early 2025.

unit: USD collected as a ransom in one case
summary: Amnesty records ransom payments of around $25-$46 demanded for the release of detained miners.

unit: USD agreed for one week underground (paid about USD 4.31)
summary: One Rubaya digger was promised 70,000 Congolese francs (a little over $30) for a week of work; after a beating he was given 10,000 francs ($4.31).

place: Fizi territory incl. Misisi and Ngoma (South Kivu)
unit: Congolese francs maximum fine for release (from 2,000,000)
summary: The Wazalendo coalition CNPSC runs a parallel tax system and courts mainly for mining disputes, with detention; former detainees said release depended on fines of FC 2-5 million. It has issued closure orders for mining sites.

Wazalendo groups run an expanding roadblock network in South Kivu where civilians must pay high fees and face extortion, sexual violence and summary execution. Wazalendo factions fought each other over illegal taxation revenue in Uvira by Dec 2025.
CODECO-URDPC extorts thousands of dollars a month from semi-mechanised gold operators, taxes miners and runs protection rackets; artisanal miners around Mabanga pay Zaïre and then CRP/FRP.

unit: USD per month per cooperative
summary: Zaïre commander Baraka Maki Amos imposed monthly fees of $3,000 on gold cooperatives in Mabanga.

place: M23-controlled mining areas incl. Rubaya and South Kivu gold mines
summary: In its 28 Oct 2026 designation of Rwanda's defence ministry and Zigama, the US Treasury stated that civilians in M23-held mining areas face forced labour, dangerous working conditions and illegal 'taxation'. The designation targets the MoD and Zigama; the forced-labour statement is Treasury's finding in that action.

place: Rumangabo and Tshanzu camps (Rutshuru, North Kivu)
summary: HRW found thousands of forcibly recruited men, and some women and children, were made to do hard labour (digging, clearing roads, cutting wood, carrying supplies) at M23 training camps; former detainees described frequent deaths and executions of those who tried to flee.

unit: victims of 19 abuses (112 women, 30 men, 16 children), most forced labour
summary: MONUSCO attributed 19 abuses against 158 people in Ituri to CODECO in this period, most of the victims subjected to forced labour. Not stated to be at mines.

place: Rubaya and villages in Masisi, Nyiragongo, Rutshuru
summary: HRW found M23 made village and household-cluster leaders supply lists of men, sometimes ten a week; in Rubaya fighters took a leader's son when they could not find him. Recruits included children as young as 12.

place: North Kivu 1,166,859; South Kivu 1,094,130; Ituri 1,011,568; Tanganyika 270,358
unit: IDPs in four eastern provinces
summary: IOM DTM counted 3.54 million IDPs in the four eastern provinces (67% of 5.29 million nationally). South Kivu fell 11% from 1,232,251 in the previous round; North Kivu stayed flat. Returnees: 1.75 million in North Kivu, 1.15 million in South Kivu.

perpetrator: n/a (M23 accused of ignoring safety rules)
unit: bodies recovered (at least); local sources said over 50
summary: A cascade of landslides buried about ten gold pits at Lomera. Radio Okapi reported at least 10 bodies recovered; Mines.cd cited local sources saying over 50 died, including children and pregnant women, among about 100 diggers. Civil society blamed M23 for ignoring mining-code safety rules. No official toll.

unit: deaths (conflicting: 17 / >300 / >700)
summary: A June 2025 landslide at a Rubaya site was reported with widely conflicting tolls: 17 dead including women and children (Mines.cd), over 300 (Peace News Network), over 700 (DeskEco, citing local sources). Treat as unverified; no official figure found.

unit: deaths (more than)
summary: HRW reports the 28 Jan 2026 landslide at the M23-controlled Rubaya coltan mine killed more than 200 people, including women and children, many buried alive after rain collapsed artisanal shafts. Toll already in seed from BBC and others.

unit: several deaths (no toll)
summary: Another collapse was reported at the Gakombe site in Rubaya four days after the 3 Mar disaster, burying several diggers; there was no official toll.

unit: % of mining sites with FARDC interference (42% of miners)
summary: IPIS found the FARDC interfered at 37% of 829 visited mining sites (employing 42% of miners), more than non-state armed groups (29%). Overall, 52% of sites and 61% of miners were affected by armed interference.

unit: % of Shabunda sites illegally taxed by FARDC/PNC (90 of 139)
summary: In Shabunda, 90 of 139 sites (86% of miners) paid illegal taxes to FARDC and police. Soldiers took about $30 a week per dredge plus about $0.50 a week per miner, and FARDC roadblocks on the Kamituga road charged travellers about $0.50 each.

unit: roadblocks mapped (FARDC operated 48, 44%)
summary: A 2023 IPIS/DIIS/ASSODIP study mapped 110 roadblocks in Masisi (84) and Walikale (26); the FARDC ran 48 of them, and 16% sat on roads mainly used for mineral transport.

unit: abuses attributed to Wazalendo (M23: 503)
summary: UN human-rights monitors attributed 221 abuses against 573 victims to Wazalendo, second only to AFC/M23 (503 abuses against 1,648 victims), out of 1,555 violations nationwide. Not mine-specific.

place: Masisi (North Kivu), Kabare (South Kivu), Goma, Bukavu
unit: survivors of gang rape by Wazalendo interviewed (8 by M23)
summary: Amnesty interviewed 14 gang-rape survivors: 8 attributed to M23, 5 to Wazalendo (4 in Masisi, 1 in Kabare), and others to FARDC. Not mine-specific.

unit: % of artisanal labour force aged under 15 (about 1,098 children)
summary: At 41 gold sites in western Mambasa, IPIS found children under 15 working at 51% of sites, about 1,098 children or 8% of workers; counting indirect work, child labour was present at 70% of sites. Tasks included digging pits and handling mercury. Women were 3% of the workforce.
